morning_concept: 🧠 Do you know how a distributed lock actually works?
morning_concept_explanation:
## Why do we need one?

Imagine your API runs on 10 servers. Two requests arrive at almost the same time and both need to modify the same shared resource.

A normal in-process mutex (a lock that only coordinates threads inside one process) cannot help:

```text
Request A → Server 1 → lock 🔒
Request B → Server 2 → lock 🔒

They hold different locks.
Both think they are allowed to continue.
```

A distributed lock is a coordination mechanism where multiple processes agree that only one of them should own a resource at a time.

## The mental model

Think of the lock as a shared lease:

```text
Client A
   │
   │ acquire(resource)
   ▼
Lock service
   │
   ├── free → grant A
   └── owned → reject/wait
```

A TTL (time-to-live) gives the lock an expiration so a crashed client does not hold it forever.

The important idea: the lock is about coordinating ownership of a shared resource across independent processes.

## A concrete example

Suppose two workers can process the same scheduled job.

```text
Worker A ──┐
           ├── process job 42
Worker B ──┘
```

With a lock:

```text
Worker A ── acquire(job:42) ──► granted
Worker B ── acquire(job:42) ──► rejected

Worker A ── process ──► release
Worker B ── retry ──► granted
```

With Redis, a simple single-instance pattern uses an atomic SET with NX (only create the key if it does not exist) and PX (set an expiration time):

```redis
SET lock:job:42 <unique-token> NX PX 30000
```

The unique token matters when releasing the lock: a slow client must not delete a lock that another client acquired after the first lock expired.

## The part that makes it hard

Imagine:

```text
1. A acquires lock
2. A starts slow work
3. lock expires
4. B acquires lock
5. A wakes up
6. A continues writing
```

Now A and B can both touch the resource.

This is why “I added a Redis lock” is not automatically a complete correctness story.

A fencing token (a monotonically increasing ownership number that the protected resource can reject when it is stale) can prevent an old owner from continuing to modify the resource.

## Trade-offs

```text
More coordination
      ↓
Better control over shared work
      ↓
More latency
More failure modes
More operational complexity
```

And sometimes you do not need a distributed lock. If the real requirement is “only one database row may be updated,” an atomic database operation or transaction can be safer and simpler.

## Where you see it

Scheduled jobs, duplicate work prevention, resource reservation, cache rebuilding, and ownership of shared work are common examples.

## Interview connection

Distributed locking naturally appears in system-design questions involving contention, such as two users trying to reserve the same resource. Candidate discussions show interviewers probing whether a database transaction or constraint, optimistic locking, pessimistic locking, or a distributed lock is actually appropriate.

## Takeaway

```text
What must be exclusive?
        ↓
Can the source of truth enforce it?
        ↓
If not, what lock/lease mechanism?
        ↓
What if the owner crashes or gets slow?
        ↓
How do we stop stale owners from writing?
```

Sources: Redis distributed locks; Google SRE.
evening_feedback:
## The useful interview pattern

Concurrency questions often become interesting when the interviewer changes the failure model.

```text
Two requests modify one resource
          ↓
Use a database transaction
          ↓
Now there are multiple application servers
          ↓
Now the worker can crash
          ↓
Now the lock can expire
          ↓
What stops the old worker from writing?
```

The important lesson is that “distributed lock” is not the answer by itself. You need to explain what invariant you are protecting and what happens when the coordinator, client, network, or lease fails.

### What to practice

- What exactly must be mutually exclusive?
- Can the database enforce it atomically?
- What happens if the owner crashes?
- What happens if the work takes longer than the lease?
- Can a stale owner still modify the resource?

Those questions are more valuable than memorizing one Redis recipe.

⚠️ Candidate reports are signals, not guarantees of a particular interview.
